summary: Provides recommendations for the functionality of Internet Fax Gateways, which connect the telephone-network fax service to email-based Internet fax. An offramp gateway sends from Internet fax to a phone fax machine, and an onramp gateway does the reverse. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A bridge helps you cross a river. This memo describes what a bridge between regular fax machines and email-based fax should do so pages go safely both ways.

questions: how does address translation work in fax gateways
what image format does internet fax use
how do fax gateways handle errors
subtitle: How to bridge the gap between telephone fax and email-based Internet fax.

tldr.problem: Internet fax systems (which send documents via email as image files) and traditional telephone network fax machines use incompatible technologies and cannot send documents to each other without conversion.
tldr.mechanism: Internet Fax Gateways convert messages and addresses between the two systems: an offramp gateway converts from email fax to telephone fax, and an onramp gateway does the reverse. Each must handle address translation, image format conversion and error notification.
tldr.outcome: The two fax systems can interoperate, allowing users of each to send documents to users of the other. This was important as email-based fax became more popular.

facts.label: Gateway types
facts.value: 2: offramp (email to phone) and onramp (phone to email)

today: RFC 4160 is an Informational RFC from 2005 and has not been obsoleted. While its focus on bridging telephone and email fax systems reflects a transitional period when both technologies were in common use, the recommendations remain relevant for any system that must convert between the two.

sections.title: The Problem of Two Fax Systems
sections.content:
By the early 2000s, there were two competing ways to send facsimiles over long distances. The traditional system used the General Switched Telephone Network (GSTN), the public switched telephone network, to transmit fax documents directly between fax machines. Meanwhile, Internet Fax (i-fax) was emerging as an alternative, sending fax documents as MIME email messages over IP networks, with image data in a standard format such as TIFF.

The problem was that a user connected to the telephone network fax system could not easily send a document to a user connected to the Internet fax system, and vice versa. This document provides recommendations for Internet Fax Gateways that bridge these two systems, allowing documents to pass between them.
sections.eli5: Some people still had old fax machines plugged into the phone line. New people were using email to send faxes. The gateway translates between these two systems so everyone can communicate.

sections.title: Address Translation Between Fax Systems
sections.content:
The two fax systems use different address formats. In the telephone network, fax destinations are phone numbers such as +44 116 496 0348. In Internet fax, destinations are email addresses such as user@example.com.

An offramp gateway (sending from Internet fax to GSTN) must convert email addresses to phone numbers. It MUST extract the left-hand side of the email address and look up or translate it to a phone number. The phone number must then be converted to a local-phone format appropriate for the gateway's local telephone network (for example, removing the international prefix if it is local, or adding the correct exit-code for international dialing).

An onramp gateway (receiving from GSTN) must do the reverse. It can receive a phone number from a GSTN fax machine (often entered by the user via DTMF tones), encode it as a global-phone address, and construct an Internet fax email address. The gateway MAY also support indirect address mapping, where a user enters a short number (like 1234) that the gateway looks up in a local table to find the actual email address.

Both gateways should also handle subaddress information, a feature that allows further routing at the destination fax machine, using ITU standard T.33.
sections.eli5: The gateway reads an email address and figures out what phone number it means. Or it reads a phone number and figures out what email address to send to. It also handles special codes for reaching a specific department in a building.

sections.title: Image Format Conversion
sections.content:
The two systems represent fax images in different formats. GSTN fax machines use a format defined by ITU-T recommendations, with specific requirements for image resolution and compression. Internet fax documents use TIFF Profile-S, a standard image format designed for fax transmission over email.

Offramp gateways MUST convert from TIFF Profile-S to the GSTN fax format. Onramp gateways MUST convert from GSTN fax format to TIFF Profile-S. This conversion must preserve the image quality and handle variations in how different fax machines and email systems encode the image data.
sections.eli5: A fax machine and an email both need to understand the picture. The gateway reads one format and rewrites it in the other, like translating a book.

sections.title: Error Handling and Delivery Notifications
sections.content:
Fax transmission can fail for many reasons: the destination number is wrong, the fax machine is busy, the connection drops, or the document cannot be delivered. Both gateway types MUST provide error notification to inform the originator that the transmission failed.

An offramp gateway that fails to deliver to a GSTN fax destination SHOULD send a Message Delivery Notification (MDN) back to the Internet fax originator, using the disposition-type "processed" and the disposition-modifier "error" to indicate that an error occurred. If the gateway cannot send the MDN (for example, if it cannot reach the originator's mail server), it MAY log the error and notify an administrator.

An onramp gateway that receives an error notification from the Internet fax destination (such as a bounce message indicating the address does not exist) MAY forward a readable error notice back to the GSTN sender via a GSTN fax sent through an offramp gateway, if such a gateway is available. Otherwise, the error information may be logged.
sections.eli5: If a fax doesn't get through, the gateway sends a message back saying 'Sorry, I couldn't deliver this.' It tries hard to tell the person who sent it, and if it can't, it keeps a record.

sections.title: User Authorization
sections.content:
Both gateway types MAY implement optional authorization functions to prevent unauthorized users from sending faxes through the gateway, which could incur costs.

An offramp gateway receives Internet fax as email messages, which MAY be digitally signed using S/MIME or OpenPGP standards. The gateway can verify the signature and check whether the user is authorized to send faxes to the GSTN network. If authorization fails, it MUST generate an error notification and return the message to the sender.

An onramp gateway MAY use DTMF (Dual Tone Multi-Frequency) tones, Caller-ID information from the GSTN, or a local authorization table to verify that the GSTN fax sender is allowed to use the gateway. If authorization fails, it MUST generate an error message for the sender. This prevents unauthorized (and costly) use of the gateway.
sections.eli5: Before letting someone send a fax through the gateway, it checks if they are allowed to. Email faxes can be signed like a contract. Phone faxes can be checked against a list of approved users.
